title: Clara Schumann Holds Her Family Together
text:
Clara Wieck was a celebrated concert pianist from her childhood. In 1840, after a court battle against her own father, she married the composer Robert Schumann. They had eight children, and she kept performing while raising them, often championing her husband's music.

In February 1854 Robert, tormented by mental illness, threw himself into the Rhine. He was rescued and, at his own request, taken to an asylum at Endenich near Bonn. Clara was pregnant with their eighth child. The doctors kept her from visiting him for more than two years; she saw him again only in July 1856, in the last days before he died. The young Johannes Brahms, who had become a close friend of the family, helped look after the household during these years.

With seven children to support, Clara went back to the concert stage. For four decades she toured Germany, the rest of Europe and England, earning the family's living and making her husband's works known. She also edited his compositions, and from 1878 taught at the conservatory in Frankfurt.

Her family life brought more sorrow. A son spent his life in an asylum, a daughter and two more sons died before her, and she took in the children of her son Ferdinand. Her diaries record exhaustion and grief, but also her determination to work. She died in 1896, one of the great musicians of her century.
lesson: When disaster strikes a family, steady work can be both a living and a refuge. Resilience is often less a feeling than a daily choice to keep going.
people: Clara Schumann, Robert Schumann, Johannes Brahms
source: Clara Schumann's diaries and letters; Nancy B. Reich, Clara Schumann: The Artist and the Woman (1985)
